Field studies of Trachyphonus darnaudii in the savannah woodlands of East Africa have provided detailed insights into its early developmental physiology. Eggs incubated at a controlled temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C] hatch after an incubation period of 15.3 days [ab = 15.3 days], a duration that aligns closely with the developmental rates observed in other lybiid barbets. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings emerge at a remarkably small size, with an initial wet body mass of just 4.2 grams [Ww0 = 4.2 grams]. This figure, consistent with extrapolations from the congener Lybius torquatus, underscores the substantial energetic investment required during the subsequent nestling phase. The hatchlings are completely dependent on biparental provisioning, and their early growth trajectory is characterized by rapid mass accumulation driven by a diet of insects and soft fruits delivered by both parents. This initial mass represents a critical starting point for the pronounced developmental changes that occur before fledging.

Breeding adults exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism in their ultimate body size, a pattern documented through extensive capture-mark-recapture efforts across multiple breeding seasons. Females attain a maximum adult wet body mass of 46.4 grams [Wwi = 46.4 grams], whereas males are slightly smaller, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 45.8 grams [Wwi = 45.8 grams]. This difference, though modest, is consistent across populations and likely reflects differential energetic demands associated with egg production and incubation duties. The relatively small mass difference between sexes is typical of monogamous cavity-nesting species where both parents share incubation and provisioning roles. These asymptotic masses are achieved after the completion of somatic growth, well before the onset of reproductive activity, and serve as a baseline for understanding the species' metabolic scaling and reproductive investment.

Under the typical thermal regime of active metabolic periods for Trachyphonus darnaudii, which centers on an ambient temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], several key life-history milestones have been quantified through longitudinal monitoring of marked individuals. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at 28 days after hatching [tx = 28 days after hatching], a period of rapid feather development and neuromuscular coordination at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. Sexual maturity, marking the onset of gonadal development and the capacity to breed, is attained at 84 days after hatching [tp = 84 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This relatively short interval to puberty is characteristic of small-bodied African barbets and allows for recruitment into the breeding population within a single calendar year, an important adaptation for a species occupying seasonally variable environments.

Longitudinal data from a nine-year field study in southern Kenya provide a comprehensive picture of the species' reproductive scheduling and lifespan. First successful reproduction, defined by the laying of a viable clutch, occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], indicating that most individuals delay breeding until their second calendar year at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. The species exhibits a low maximum annual reproductive output, with females laying a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], which typically contains between 2 and 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 2 and 4 eggs per clutch]. This conservative reproductive strategy, combined with the energetic constraints of cavity excavation and extended parental care, limits the annual recruitment potential. Maximum documented longevity in the wild reaches 13 years [am = 13 years], a substantial lifespan for a bird of this body size, reflecting low adult mortality rates typical of tropical forest and savannah specialists at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C].

Respirometry trials conducted on post-absorptive, resting individuals during the inactive phase of their daily cycle have characterized the species' metabolic demands. At a chamber temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate was recorded at 39.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 39.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This rate, measured during the thermoneutral zone for the species, represents the minimum energetic cost of maintaining physiological homeostasis in a non-digesting, non-reproductive adult. An adult female asymptotic mass of 46.4 grams [Wwi = 46.4 grams] and a slightly lower male value of 45.8 grams [Wwi = 45.8 grams] are consistent with allometric predictions for a tropical passerine or near-passerine. When contextualized against the species' maximum recorded lifespan of 13 years [am = 13 years] and its single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] of up to 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = up to 4 eggs per clutch], this metabolic rate suggests a relatively slow pace of life, consistent with the life-history syndrome observed in many long-lived tropical bird species that invest heavily in self-maintenance and adult survival at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C].
